screens.title: Building Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs)
screens.narratorSegment: A DAO is an organization where rules are encoded on smart contracts and decisions happen by member votes rather than a central authority. In this chapter you will learn what makes a DAO different from a traditional organization, how common governance mechanisms work, and how to assemble a basic, secure DAO using OpenZeppelin building blocks. We will also walk through a deployment and a sample proposal lifecycle so you can see governance in action on a local network. Understanding these pieces matters because a DAO manages real assets and powers protocol upgrades; design choices affect fairness, security, and the ability of the community to respond to mistakes. As an example, you will see how a governance token grants voting rights, why a timelock provides a safety window, and how a Governor contract coordinates proposals. By the end you will be able to design a minimal DAO, recognize common pitfalls like too-short voting periods or missing timelocks, and run a simulated proposal to observe queueing and execution. Keep a security-first mindset: design, test, and iterate before handing control to a wide community.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Building DAOs
Building Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs)
Encode rules as smart contracts, let members vote, and secure execution with time-delays and tested modules.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Orientation

You will learn DAO principles, compare governance mechanisms like token-weighted and delegated voting, and assemble a minimal DAO using OpenZeppelin's ERC20Votes, TimelockController, and Governor contracts. We'll close with a practical deployment and a simulated proposal lifecycle so you can observe propose → vote → queue → execute in a reproducible environment.

Why this matters
DAOs transfer trust from individuals to code. When designed well, they enable collective control, transparent decision-making, and safer upgrades. Poor design risks plutocracy or catastrophic exploits.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to define a DAO and explain its core principles such as transparency, decentralization, and community ownership. You will understand several governance mechanisms — token-weighted voting, quadratic and conviction voting, and delegation — and the trade-offs each one entails. You will learn to use OpenZeppelin's modular contracts to implement a minimal DAO architecture that includes an ERC20Votes governance token, a TimelockController, and a Governor contract. Finally, you will design and execute a simple governance proposal within a simulated environment using a Hardhat script, observing propose, vote, queue, and execute stages. Concrete skills include delegating votes, configuring voting period and quorum, and recognizing typical configuration mistakes that weaken security. These objectives matter because running a DAO without these fundamentals risks centralization, economic capture, or irreversible losses; the skills you gain let you design governance that balances participation, responsiveness, and safety, and to test proposals before production deployment.

screens.title: Skills & Assessment Focus
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter emphasizes practical skills and a single hands-on assessment: deploy a minimal DAO locally and run a proposal. You will practice deploying an ERC20Votes token, setting up a TimelockController with a deliberate delay, and deploying a Governor configured with voting delay, voting period, and quorum fraction. The assessment will confirm you can: delegate votes so addresses have voting power, create a proposal that encodes a function call, advance blocks to start the voting window, cast votes, and queue and execute a passed proposal through the timelock. We will also evaluate your ability to reason about security: explain why a timelock matters, identify risks from low quorum or short voting periods, and propose mitigations such as progressive decentralization and audits. A concrete example you will run is minting a small amount of governance tokens to a test account via a passed proposal. This demonstrates end-to-end control flow from proposal creation to on-chain execution while illustrating the safety buffer the timelock provides.

screens.title: What is a DAO?
screens.narratorSegment: A Decentralized Autonomous Organization is an entity whose rules and decision-making flows are encoded as smart contracts, and whose members vote to approve actions rather than relying on a central authority. Think of a DAO as a code-based constitution for a community: proposals are written, members vote according to their delegated voting power, and approved proposals are executed by contract logic. For a concrete example, imagine a small protocol treasury controlled by a DAO. Members with governance tokens can propose allocating funds to a bug bounty. If the proposal passes and meets quorum, it is queued in a timelock and executed after the delay, transferring funds to the bounty account. Contrast this with a traditional nonprofit where a board votes and a single executive executes decisions; a DAO replaces that single executor with deterministic contract code, reducing human central points of failure. A common misconception is that DAOs remove all governance complexity; in reality they shift complexity from legal and organizational structures into smart-contract design and token-economics. You must choose voting rules, timelock parameters, and role permissions carefully. Key takeaway: a DAO formalizes governance on-chain, enabling transparency and permissionless coordination, but it requires careful design and testing to avoid centralization or security failures.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › What is a DAO?
Definition & Core Idea

A DAO is an organization whose rules are encoded as smart contracts and whose members make decisions by voting. This makes governance transparent and permissionless while relying on code to execute decisions.

Analogy
Like a constitution implemented in code: proposals are legislative acts, voting is the parliament, and contracts execute laws.
Concrete example
A protocol treasury DAO votes to fund a bug bounty; passed proposal transfers funds after a timelock delay.
Common misconception
DAOs remove governance complexity. In truth, they reframe it into contract and token design, which require testing and careful parameter choices.
Key Takeaway

DAOs make governance code-visible and enforceable on-chain, but safe DAO design requires explicit trade-offs and security measures.

Quick architecture callout
Governance Token
Holds voting power via delegation.
Governor
Proposes and counts votes.
Timelock
Delays execution for safety.
Understanding the interaction between token, governor, and timelock is the foundation of building any DAO. The follow-up screens unpack governance mechanisms and the OpenZeppelin modules that implement them.
Try this
Sketch a governance flow for a small DAO: what roles do token holders play, who can propose, and what actions should be timelocked?

screens.title: DAO Principles: Transparency, Decentralization, Ownership
screens.narratorSegment: Three principles guide DAO design: transparency, decentralization, and community ownership. Transparency means proposals and votes are visible on-chain, which builds trust but also requires careful privacy considerations when sensitive information is involved. Decentralization reduces single points of control; however, decentralization is a spectrum and requires governance parameter tuning to avoid concentration of power. Community ownership refers to aligning incentives so the token-holding community benefits from protocol success; this can be achieved through token distribution, vesting, and active delegation. For example, if a protocol mints tokens only to a tiny founding team, token-weighted voting can concentrate power and mimic centralized control. That outcome is often undesirable. Design choices such as quorum thresholds, voting periods, and delegation mechanisms determine how easy it is for proposals to pass and how quickly a DAO can react. A short voting period may enable rapid response but increases the risk of low participation and rushed decisions. A too-small quorum allows decisions by a few actors. Practical trade-offs include progressive decentralization: start centrally to move quickly, then widen participation and reduce administrative keys as the community grows. Always plan migration paths and prioritize audits, because code changes and treasury actions are permanent once executed.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › DAO Principles
Core Principles
Transparency, decentralization, and community ownership guide every DAO decision.
Transparency
On-chain proposals and votes build trust and auditability. Consider privacy trade-offs for sensitive actions.
Decentralization
Reduces single points of control but requires mechanisms to prevent power concentration.
Ownership
Token allocation and delegation patterns determine who benefits and who governs.
Trade-off example
Short voting period enables fast decisions but risks low participation and rushed mistakes.
Warning
Concentrated token distribution with token-weighted voting can create plutocracy.
Progressive Decentralization
Start with guarded, centralized controls while the protocol matures. Gradually hand over roles and permissions as the community grows and audits confirm safety.
Key Takeaway
Balance responsiveness and safety: design voting periods, quorum, and token distribution to match the DAO's maturity and threat model.

screens.title: Common Governance Mechanisms
screens.narratorSegment: There are several governance mechanisms used in DAOs, each with different incentives and vulnerabilities. Token-weighted voting is the simplest: voting power is proportional to token holdings. It is straightforward to implement but can lead to plutocracy, where large holders dominate decisions. Quadratic voting reduces the marginal power of large holders by making the cost of additional influence grow faster; this helps amplify minority preferences but is more complex and can be gamed without careful design. Conviction voting accumulates strength for a position over time, rewarding sustained support and making quick flips harder; however, it requires continuous participation and careful parameterization. Delegated voting lets token holders delegate their voting power to trusted representatives, improving participation and expertise in governance, but it introduces representative centralization if many delegates accumulate large shares of voting power. For a practical example: if a DAO needs to decide a treasury allocation, token-weighted voting may favor the largest funders, quadratic voting could let passionate small holders push a niche grant, and delegated voting could produce more expert scrutiny if delegates are reputable. A common misconception is that one mechanism is universally best; in practice choose the mechanism that aligns with your governance goals and token distribution, and test with conservative parameters.

keyIdea.text: Choose voting mechanisms to match your goals: simplicity vs. fairness vs. engagement. No one-size-fits-all solution.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Governance Mechanisms
Compare Voting Systems
Understand strengths and failure modes so you can pick a scheme that matches your DAO's goals.
Token-weighted voting
Simple and gas-efficient. Risk: wealth concentration may lead to plutocracy.
Quadratic voting
Reduces large-holder advantage by making extra votes costlier. Risk: complexity and potential for vote-purchase attacks if tokens are fungible with economic value.
Conviction voting
Votes accumulate strength over time, rewarding persistent support. Risk: lower responsiveness and higher parameter complexity.
Delegated voting
Improves participation by delegating to trusted representatives. Risk: representative centralization and delegation capture.
Scenario
A DAO votes on a grant to a small research team. Token-weighted voting favors large backers. Quadratic voting gives small, enthusiastic contributors more influence; conviction voting could let sustained support win over a short opposition surge; delegated voting could concentrate review to trusted delegates who evaluate the grant thoroughly.
Design tip
Combine mechanisms or tune parameters: you might use token-weighted voting with a higher quorum and allow delegation to reputable delegates for technical proposals.
Key Takeaway
Mechanisms trade simplicity for fairness and responsiveness. Choose intentionally and test conservatively.

screens.title: OpenZeppelin Building Blocks for DAOs
screens.narratorSegment: OpenZeppelin offers modular, audited components that simplify DAO construction. The three primary pieces you will use together are: ERC20Votes, TimelockController, and Governor. ERC20Votes is an ERC-20 extension that tracks historical voting snapshots and supports delegation so token holders can assign voting power. The Governor contract manages proposals, enforces voting delays and periods, counts votes, and interacts with a TimelockController to queue and execute actions. The TimelockController acts as a gatekeeper: it holds execution rights and imposes a configurable minimum delay before operations can be executed. In practice you deploy the ERC20Votes token, mint or distribute tokens, and ensure holders delegate to themselves or delegates. Then deploy a TimelockController with a sensible delay, and finally deploy a Governor configured with votingDelay, votingPeriod, and quorum. The Governor is granted proposer role on the timelock and typically the timelock is configured so that the Governor is the timelock admin; this ensures only proposals passed through the Governor can schedule executions. A frequent pitfall is misconfigured roles that leave the timelock controllable by the deployer. Always grant the Governor the proposer role and remove unnecessary admin keys from deployer accounts.

keyIdea.text: Token provides votes, Governor runs proposals and voting, Timelock delays execution — grant roles carefully and remove deployer admin privileges.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › OpenZeppelin Blocks
Key Components
ERC20Votes
Token with voting snapshots and delegation support. It lets the Governor read voting power at a historical block.
TimelockController
Holds execution power and enforces a minimum delay between queueing and execution.
Governor
Creates proposals, counts votes, and schedules successful proposals on the timelock for execution.
Role wiring
Correct role assignment is essential. Grant the Governor proposer and admin roles on the Timelock when appropriate, and revoke deployer admin privileges to avoid centralized control.
Quick checklist
  • Deploy token and delegate votes.
  • Deploy timelock with minDelay and initial roles.
  • Deploy governor with voting parameters and grant it proposer role.
  • Revoke deployer admin roles and grant governor timelock admin if required.
Key Takeaway
OpenZeppelin modules reduce risk, but incorrect wiring of roles and delays is a frequent source of vulnerabilities.

screens.title: ERC20Votes Token (MyToken.sol)
screens.narratorSegment: ERC20Votes extends a standard ERC-20 token with voting capabilities by tracking historical vote snapshots and supporting delegation. In the provided MyToken example, the constructor mints an initial supply to the deployer and the contract inherits ERC20Votes and Ownable. Two internal hook overrides, after-token-transfer and before-token-transfer, are required to maintain proper vote accounting when tokens move. The token also exposes a mint function restricted to the owner, which in a DAO context is often controlled by a timelock or governance mechanism instead of a single admin. Delegation is crucial: holders must delegate their tokens to themselves or a delegate to enable voting power to be used by the Governor contract. Snapshots make it possible for the Governor to query voting power at the block when the proposal snapshot was taken, preventing vote manipulation that happens after votes are cast. A common misconception is that token transfer alone updates voting power for past proposals; snapshots ensure consistent historical voting tallies. When you deploy MyToken during the hands-on exercise, mint responsibly and ensure delegation calls are made so accounts have practical voting power for testing proposals.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › ERC20Votes Walkthrough
MyToken highlights
The contract inherits ERC20Votes and Ownable, mints an initial supply, and provides a mint function for the owner.
Snapshot hooks
_afterTokenTransfer and _beforeTokenTransfer are overridden to keep vote accounting accurate when balances change.
Delegation
Delegation enables an address's voting power. Call delegate to activate voting power for proposals.
Owner-controlled mint
Minting is restricted to the owner; in a DAO you should manage minting through governance or timelock roles.
Key Takeaway
Use delegation and snapshots to ensure voting power is computed at the correct block for each proposal.
Code excerpt (illustrative)
// constructor mints initial tokens
constructor(address initialOwner) ERC20("MyGovernanceToken","MGT") Ownable(initialOwner) {
    _mint(initialOwner, 1_000_000 * 10 ** decimals());
}

// Hooks required for ERC20Votes
function _afterTokenTransfer(address from, address to, uint256 amount) internal override(ERC20Votes, ERC20) {
    super._afterTokenTransfer(from, to, amount);
}

function _beforeTokenTransfer(address from, address to, uint256 amount) internal override(ERC20Votes, ERC20) {
    super._beforeTokenTransfer(from, to, amount);
}

// Owner-only mint helper
function mint(address to, uint256 amount) public onlyOwner {
    _mint(to, amount);
}
Note: This snippet is illustrative. In practice, prefer granting minting through timelock or governor-controlled privileges to decentralize power.

screens.title: TimelockController and Security
screens.narratorSegment: The TimelockController is a simple but powerful security primitive: it holds execution authority for operations and enforces a configurable minimum delay between queueing and execution. This delay provides a grace period during which the community can react if a malicious or erroneous proposal is queued. For example, if a proposal to transfer treasury funds passes unexpectedly, a timelock gives time to flag the proposal, alert exchanges and auditors, or initiate emergency countermeasures. Key timelock parameters include the minimum delay and the set of proposers and executors. Proposers are allowed to schedule operations; executors can trigger execution once the delay elapses. In many designs the Governor is granted proposer role and possibly timelock admin, while executors are set to a zero address meaning anyone can execute after the delay. A common mistake is leaving deployer accounts with admin privileges on the timelock, which preserves centralized control despite the governance layer; revoke these rights once roles are transferred to on-chain governance. Another mistake is setting an insufficient timelock, which reduces the community's time to respond. Balance your timelock length with the need for responsiveness and the expected severity of possible governance risks.

keyIdea.title: Timelock role
keyIdea.text: A timelock provides a community response window: grant roles to the Governor, remove deployer admin rights, and choose a delay that balances safety and responsiveness.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › TimelockController
Timelock essentials
The timelock holds execution rights and enforces a minimum delay. It separates approval from execution to protect the community.
Roles
Proposers schedule operations. Executors trigger them after the delay. Admins can grant or revoke roles; reduce admin keys after setup.
Min delay
Choose a delay long enough to allow response but short enough to avoid blocking routine operations.
Common pitfalls
Leaving deployer as admin or using an insufficient delay undermines the timelock's protective purpose.
Process flow (queue → execute)
When a Governor proposal passes, it is queued in the timelock. The timelock records the operation and the earliest execution time is computed by adding minDelay. After the period, anyone with executor rights can call execute and the operation runs. This separation gives the community time to react.
Example
minDelay = 1 hour. A passed proposal to transfer funds is queued; there is one hour for users to respond before execution.
Key Takeaway
A timelock is a fail-safe: configure roles and a realistic delay, and remove centralized admin privileges after governance is in place.

screens.title: Governor Contract Mechanics (MyGovernor.sol)
screens.narratorSegment: The Governor contract orchestrates proposals and voting and connects to the timelock to schedule execution. In the MyGovernor example, several OpenZeppelin extensions are composed: GovernorSettings for voting delay and period, GovernorCountingSimple for vote counting, GovernorVotes and GovernorVotesQuorumFraction for integrating ERC20Votes and quorum calculations. Important parameters include votingDelay, the number of blocks before voting starts; votingPeriod, the block length of the vote window; and quorum fraction, the percentage of supply required to validate a successful proposal. The Governor must override several functions to combine behaviors from multiple base contracts; these overrides route calls to the appropriate extension implementations and ensure consistent state. The contract also sets proposer and executor roles on the timelock and revokes unnecessary admin roles from the deployer. A common misconception is that quorum is optional; without a quorum you can pass proposals with negligible participation. In practice choose a quorum that reflects an acceptable participation minimum for legitimacy. Additionally, testing overrides and role grants in a local environment helps verify that proposals can actually be queued and executed through the timelock as intended. Governor Contract Mechanics (MyGovernor.sol) means configure voting timing and quorum, implement required overrides, and wire roles so the governor can queue and manage timelock executions.. In practical terms, voting delay, voting period, quorum, and required overrides. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Governor responsibilities
keyIdea.text: Configure voting timing and quorum, implement required overrides, and wire roles so the Governor can queue and manage timelock executions.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Governor Mechanics
Important settings
Tune votingDelay, votingPeriod, and quorum to align with governance goals and expected participation.
Voting delay
Blocks to wait after proposing before voting starts. Use a delay to allow notice and to prevent instant flash proposals.
Voting period
Duration of the voting window. Balance speed and participation.
Quorum
Minimum fraction of supply required to pass a proposal. Without quorum, decisions may lack legitimacy.
Code notes
constructor(MyToken _token, MyTimelock _timelock)
  Governor("MyGovernor")
  GovernorSettings(100, 1000, 0)
  GovernorVotes(_token)
  GovernorVotesQuorumFraction(4) { ... }

// Overrides for multiple inheritance
function votingDelay() public view override returns (uint256) { return super.votingDelay(); }

function votingPeriod() public view override returns (uint256) { return super.votingPeriod(); }

function quorum(uint256 blockNumber) public view override returns (uint256) { return super.quorum(blockNumber); }
These overrides are necessary to resolve method inheritance and preserve extension behavior. The quorum fraction of 4 means 4% of total supply is required in the provided example.
Key Takeaway
Governor configuration and correct overrides ensure voting behaves predictably and integrates with ERC20Votes and the timelock.

screens.title: Proposal Lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: A proposal goes through four main stages: propose, vote, queue, and execute. First, a member creates a proposal that encodes an intended action, such as calling a mint function on a token contract. The Governor records the proposal and, after the configured voting delay, opens the voting period. During the voting period token holders or their delegates cast votes for or against. After voting closes, the Governor tallies the votes and checks the quorum requirement. If the proposal passes, it is queued in the TimelockController; the timelock calculates the earliest execution time by adding the minimum delay. Once the delay elapses, an executor can call execute and the queued operations run. For a concrete walkthrough: create a proposal to mint tokens to an address, wait for the voting delay, cast votes from several delegated addresses, let the period finish, queue the passed proposal, advance time to pass the timelock, and execute. Misconception check: a passed proposal is not immediately executed unless there is no timelock; the timelock intentionally creates a gap for community response. The core insight is that the timelock and the Governor together enforce an auditable, time-bound decision flow that the community can verify and react to.

keyIdea.text: Propose, vote, and if passed queue in a timelock. Execution only occurs after the configured delay, providing a response window.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Proposal Lifecycle
Stages
Propose
Create an action with targets and calldata.
Vote
Token holders cast votes during the voting period.
Queue
If passed, schedule on the timelock.
Execute
After the delay, the operation is executed on-chain.
Example: Proposal to mint 1,000 tokens to a test address. Propose the mint, wait voting delay, cast votes, confirm quorum and tally, queue the proposal to the timelock, wait minDelay, then execute to mint tokens. This demonstrates end-to-end governance control flow.
Checklist
  • Encode calldata correctly for target contract functions.
  • Advance blocks to reach voting period in tests.
  • Confirm delegates and voting power before voting.
  • Queue only passed proposals and respect timelock delay.
Key Takeaway
Execution is deliberately delayed. Use the timelock to buy time for detection and reaction to harmful proposals.

screens.title: Deploying and Testing a DAO (deployDAO.js)
screens.narratorSegment: The deploy script walks through deploying MyToken, MyTimelock, and MyGovernor, delegating votes, transferring tokens to test voters, and simulating a proposal lifecycle on a local Hardhat network. Start by deploying the governance token and delegating votes for deployer and test voters so they can participate in governance. Next deploy the TimelockController with a chosen minDelay and initial proposer and executor addresses, typically granting the deployer or governor proposer rights during setup. Deploy the Governor pointing to the token and timelock, then configure timelock roles so the Governor can propose and control the timelock. The script demonstrates creating a proposal by encoding a mint function call on the token contract; it shows how to advance blocks for voting delay and voting period by calling the provider's evm_mine method in a loop. Cast votes from multiple accounts to observe different vote outcomes. After voting finishes, check the governor's state; if successful, queue and then simulate the timelock delay by advancing time or mining additional blocks before executing. Watch logs for proposalId, state changes, and final token balances to verify execution. Misconception check: advancing blocks and time in tests is not the same as mainnet timing; use tests to validate logic before real deployment.

keyIdea.text: Deploy token, timelock, governor, delegate votes, create a proposal, advance blocks, vote, queue, advance time, and execute — observe logs and balances for verification.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Deploy & Test
Script steps
  1. Deploy MyToken and delegate votes for deployer and test voters.
  2. Transfer tokens to voter accounts for test participation.
  3. Deploy MyTimelock with minDelay, proposers, and executors.
  4. Deploy MyGovernor and grant it proposer and admin roles on the timelock.
  5. Create and propose an encoded mint transaction, advance blocks, cast votes, queue, advance time, and execute.
Simulation tips
In a local network you can advance blocks quickly with provider calls. Use this to simulate voting delays and periods deterministically. Always inspect logs for proposalId and state transitions, and check token balances after execute to confirm the payload ran.
Example snippet
// encodedFunctionCall = token.interface.encodeFunctionData("mint", [voter1.address, ethers.parseEther("1000")]);
await governor.propose(targets, values, calldatas, description);
// advance blocks, cast votes
await governor.queue(targets, values, calldatas, descriptionHash);
// advance time, execute
await governor.execute(targets, values, calldatas, descriptionHash);
Key Takeaway
Testing the full lifecycle locally is essential to validate role wiring, encoding of calldata, and correct timelock behaviour before mainnet deployment.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Security Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Building a DAO introduces specific security and design risks. Frequent mistakes include misconfigured voting parameters, insufficient timelock delays, and leaving deployer accounts with admin roles on the timelock. For example, too-short voting periods reduce participation and increase the chance that a flash attack or low turnout decides protocol-critical votes. Too-low quorum lets a small minority pass changes that affect the entire community. Role mismanagement — such as not granting the Governor proposer role, or failing to revoke deployer admin — can prevent the Governor from queueing operations or leave centralized control in place. Best practices include: choose conservative defaults and iterate, use a timelock with a realistic delay to allow response time, wire roles so only the Governor can propose and the timelock holds execution power, and perform audits before decentralizing sensitive privileges. Progressive decentralization is a recommended path: begin with more centralized control to enable fast iteration, then slowly transfer roles to on-chain governance as the community and test coverage grow. Finally, ensure clear documentation for delegates and voters so participation is informed and quorum expectations are explicit. Common Mistakes and Security Best Practices means avoid short voting windows, low quorum, and lingering deployer admin roles. prefer conservative parameters and stepwise decentralization with audits.. In practical terms, configuration errors, role mismanagement, and progressive decentralization. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Avoid short voting windows, low quorum, and lingering deployer admin roles. Prefer conservative parameters and stepwise decentralization with audits.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Mistakes & Best Practices
Common mistakes
  • Voting period too short → low participation and rushed decisions.
  • Quorum set too low → decisions by a small minority lack legitimacy.
  • Deployer retains timelock admin rights → centralization of execution control.
  • Incorrect role wiring prevents the Governor from queueing or executing proposals.
Best practices
Use conservative parameters initially, perform audits, and adopt progressive decentralization to hand over control gradually. Configure the timelock so the Governor is the proposer and remove unnecessary deployer admin roles. Document governance rules and quorum expectations to encourage informed participation.
Pro-tip
Run the full deploy and proposal test on a local network multiple times and validate logs and balances to confirm the end-to-end flow before any mainnet deployment.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three core ideas front of mind. First, a DAO encodes governance rules in smart contracts so members can transparently propose, vote, and execute actions. Second, OpenZeppelin's ERC20Votes, TimelockController, and Governor contracts form a reliable starting architecture: tokens provide voting power, the Governor manages proposals and voting, and the timelock delays execution to protect the community. Third, governance parameters like voting period and quorum materially affect security and legitimacy; test conservative settings and adopt progressive decentralization. A short practical reminder: always delegate tokens if you expect to vote, ensure the Governor has proposer rights on the timelock, and remove deployer admin privileges to avoid accidental centralization. These core concepts will guide your design and testing as you build a minimal DAO and run a proposal lifecycle in the hands-on exercise.

Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Three Quick Reminders
Delegate
Make sure token holders delegate to themselves or delegates to activate voting power.
Wire roles
Grant Governor proposer rights, timelock executor rights, and remove deployer admin keys.

fullNarratorScript:
A DAO is an organization where rules are encoded on smart contracts and decisions happen by member votes rather than a central authority. In this chapter you will learn what makes a DAO different from a traditional organization, how common governance mechanisms work, and how to assemble a basic, secure DAO using OpenZeppelin building blocks. We will also walk through a deployment and a sample proposal lifecycle so you can see governance in action on a local network. Understanding these pieces matters because a DAO manages real assets and powers protocol upgrades; design choices affect fairness, security, and the ability of the community to respond to mistakes. As an example, you will see how a governance token grants voting rights, why a timelock provides a safety window, and how a Governor contract coordinates proposals. By the end you will be able to design a minimal DAO, recognize common pitfalls like too-short voting periods or missing timelocks, and run a simulated proposal to observe queueing and execution. Keep a security-first mindset: design, test, and iterate before handing control to a wide community.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to define a DAO and explain its core principles such as transparency, decentralization, and community ownership. You will understand several governance mechanisms — token-weighted voting, quadratic and conviction voting, and delegation — and the trade-offs each one entails. You will learn to use OpenZeppelin's modular contracts to implement a minimal DAO architecture that includes an ERC20Votes governance token, a TimelockController, and a Governor contract. Finally, you will design and execute a simple governance proposal within a simulated environment using a Hardhat script, observing propose, vote, queue, and execute stages. Concrete skills include delegating votes, configuring voting period and quorum, and recognizing typical configuration mistakes that weaken security. These objectives matter because running a DAO without these fundamentals risks centralization, economic capture, or irreversible losses; the skills you gain let you design governance that balances participation, responsiveness, and safety, and to test proposals before production deployment.

This chapter emphasizes practical skills and a single hands-on assessment: deploy a minimal DAO locally and run a proposal. You will practice deploying an ERC20Votes token, setting up a TimelockController with a deliberate delay, and deploying a Governor configured with voting delay, voting period, and quorum fraction. The assessment will confirm you can: delegate votes so addresses have voting power, create a proposal that encodes a function call, advance blocks to start the voting window, cast votes, and queue and execute a passed proposal through the timelock. We will also evaluate your ability to reason about security: explain why a timelock matters, identify risks from low quorum or short voting periods, and propose mitigations such as progressive decentralization and audits. A concrete example you will run is minting a small amount of governance tokens to a test account via a passed proposal. This demonstrates end-to-end control flow from proposal creation to on-chain execution while illustrating the safety buffer the timelock provides.

A Decentralized Autonomous Organization is an entity whose rules and decision-making flows are encoded as smart contracts, and whose members vote to approve actions rather than relying on a central authority. Think of a DAO as a code-based constitution for a community: proposals are written, members vote according to their delegated voting power, and approved proposals are executed by contract logic. For a concrete example, imagine a small protocol treasury controlled by a DAO. Members with governance tokens can propose allocating funds to a bug bounty. If the proposal passes and meets quorum, it is queued in a timelock and executed after the delay, transferring funds to the bounty account. Contrast this with a traditional nonprofit where a board votes and a single executive executes decisions; a DAO replaces that single executor with deterministic contract code, reducing human central points of failure. A common misconception is that DAOs remove all governance complexity; in reality they shift complexity from legal and organizational structures into smart-contract design and token-economics. You must choose voting rules, timelock parameters, and role permissions carefully. Key takeaway: a DAO formalizes governance on-chain, enabling transparency and permissionless coordination, but it requires careful design and testing to avoid centralization or security failures.

Three principles guide DAO design: transparency, decentralization, and community ownership. Transparency means proposals and votes are visible on-chain, which builds trust but also requires careful privacy considerations when sensitive information is involved. Decentralization reduces single points of control; however, decentralization is a spectrum and requires governance parameter tuning to avoid concentration of power. Community ownership refers to aligning incentives so the token-holding community benefits from protocol success; this can be achieved through token distribution, vesting, and active delegation. For example, if a protocol mints tokens only to a tiny founding team, token-weighted voting can concentrate power and mimic centralized control. That outcome is often undesirable. Design choices such as quorum thresholds, voting periods, and delegation mechanisms determine how easy it is for proposals to pass and how quickly a DAO can react. A short voting period may enable rapid response but increases the risk of low participation and rushed decisions. A too-small quorum allows decisions by a few actors. Practical trade-offs include progressive decentralization: start centrally to move quickly, then widen participation and reduce administrative keys as the community grows. Always plan migration paths and prioritize audits, because code changes and treasury actions are permanent once executed.

There are several governance mechanisms used in DAOs, each with different incentives and vulnerabilities. Token-weighted voting is the simplest: voting power is proportional to token holdings. It is straightforward to implement but can lead to plutocracy, where large holders dominate decisions. Quadratic voting reduces the marginal power of large holders by making the cost of additional influence grow faster; this helps amplify minority preferences but is more complex and can be gamed without careful design. Conviction voting accumulates strength for a position over time, rewarding sustained support and making quick flips harder; however, it requires continuous participation and careful parameterization. Delegated voting lets token holders delegate their voting power to trusted representatives, improving participation and expertise in governance, but it introduces representative centralization if many delegates accumulate large shares of voting power. For a practical example: if a DAO needs to decide a treasury allocation, token-weighted voting may favor the largest funders, quadratic voting could let passionate small holders push a niche grant, and delegated voting could produce more expert scrutiny if delegates are reputable. A common misconception is that one mechanism is universally best; in practice choose the mechanism that aligns with your governance goals and token distribution, and test with conservative parameters.

OpenZeppelin offers modular, audited components that simplify DAO construction. The three primary pieces you will use together are: ERC20Votes, TimelockController, and Governor. ERC20Votes is an ERC-20 extension that tracks historical voting snapshots and supports delegation so token holders can assign voting power. The Governor contract manages proposals, enforces voting delays and periods, counts votes, and interacts with a TimelockController to queue and execute actions. The TimelockController acts as a gatekeeper: it holds execution rights and imposes a configurable minimum delay before operations can be executed. In practice you deploy the ERC20Votes token, mint or distribute tokens, and ensure holders delegate to themselves or delegates. Then deploy a TimelockController with a sensible delay, and finally deploy a Governor configured with votingDelay, votingPeriod, and quorum. The Governor is granted proposer role on the timelock and typically the timelock is configured so that the Governor is the timelock admin; this ensures only proposals passed through the Governor can schedule executions. A frequent pitfall is misconfigured roles that leave the timelock controllable by the deployer. Always grant the Governor the proposer role and remove unnecessary admin keys from deployer accounts.

ERC20Votes extends a standard ERC-20 token with voting capabilities by tracking historical vote snapshots and supporting delegation. In the provided MyToken example, the constructor mints an initial supply to the deployer and the contract inherits ERC20Votes and Ownable. Two internal hook overrides, after-token-transfer and before-token-transfer, are required to maintain proper vote accounting when tokens move. The token also exposes a mint function restricted to the owner, which in a DAO context is often controlled by a timelock or governance mechanism instead of a single admin. Delegation is crucial: holders must delegate their tokens to themselves or a delegate to enable voting power to be used by the Governor contract. Snapshots make it possible for the Governor to query voting power at the block when the proposal snapshot was taken, preventing vote manipulation that happens after votes are cast. A common misconception is that token transfer alone updates voting power for past proposals; snapshots ensure consistent historical voting tallies. When you deploy MyToken during the hands-on exercise, mint responsibly and ensure delegation calls are made so accounts have practical voting power for testing proposals.

The TimelockController is a simple but powerful security primitive: it holds execution authority for operations and enforces a configurable minimum delay between queueing and execution. This delay provides a grace period during which the community can react if a malicious or erroneous proposal is queued. For example, if a proposal to transfer treasury funds passes unexpectedly, a timelock gives time to flag the proposal, alert exchanges and auditors, or initiate emergency countermeasures. Key timelock parameters include the minimum delay and the set of proposers and executors. Proposers are allowed to schedule operations; executors can trigger execution once the delay elapses. In many designs the Governor is granted proposer role and possibly timelock admin, while executors are set to a zero address meaning anyone can execute after the delay. A common mistake is leaving deployer accounts with admin privileges on the timelock, which preserves centralized control despite the governance layer; revoke these rights once roles are transferred to on-chain governance. Another mistake is setting an insufficient timelock, which reduces the community's time to respond. Balance your timelock length with the need for responsiveness and the expected severity of possible governance risks.

Building a DAO introduces specific security and design risks. Frequent mistakes include misconfigured voting parameters, insufficient timelock delays, and leaving deployer accounts with admin roles on the timelock. For example, too-short voting periods reduce participation and increase the chance that a flash attack or low turnout decides protocol-critical votes. Too-low quorum lets a small minority pass changes that affect the entire community. Role mismanagement — such as not granting the Governor proposer role, or failing to revoke deployer admin — can prevent the Governor from queueing operations or leave centralized control in place. Best practices include: choose conservative defaults and iterate, use a timelock with a realistic delay to allow response time, wire roles so only the Governor can propose and the timelock holds execution power, and perform audits before decentralizing sensitive privileges. Progressive decentralization is a recommended path: begin with more centralized control to enable fast iteration, then slowly transfer roles to on-chain governance as the community and test coverage grow. Finally, ensure clear documentation for delegates and voters so participation is informed and quorum expectations are explicit.
